fact_or_fake: A day on Mercury lasts longer than a year on Mercury.
Mercury rotates so slowly that one day takes 176 Earth days, while its year is only 88 Earth days.
The human body contains enough carbon to make about 9,000 pencils.
The carbon in the human body, if extracted, would fill thousands of pencils.
Hot water freezes faster than cold water under some conditions.
This is called the Mpemba effect, observed and studied since ancient times.
The sun makes up about 99.8% of the total mass of our solar system.
Almost all the mass in our solar system is concentrated in the sun.
Sound travels faster through water than through air.
Sound moves about 4.3 times faster in water than in air due to water's density.
All mammals can swim instinctively from birth.
Many land mammals can swim without training, but not all — and some, like giraffes, struggle significantly.
A bolt of lightning contains enough energy to toast 100,000 slices of bread.
A single lightning bolt carries roughly 250 kilowatt-hours of energy — enough to power a lot of toasters.
Octopuses have blue blood.
Octopus blood contains hemocyanin (copper-based) rather than hemoglobin, making it blue.
The largest known star is about 100 times the size of our sun.
The largest known stars (like UY Scuti) are over 1,700 times the radius of our sun.
Trees communicate with each other through underground fungal networks.
Known as the 'Wood Wide Web', trees share nutrients and signals via mycorrhizal fungi.
Humans share about 60% of their DNA with bananas.
This reflects common evolutionary building blocks shared across all life on Earth.
The Sahara Desert was once covered in grassland and lakes.
Around 6,000–10,000 years ago, the Sahara experienced a 'Green Sahara' period with rivers and wildlife.
Water can exist in three states but not simultaneously.
The triple point of water allows it to exist as solid, liquid, and gas simultaneously at a specific temperature and pressure.
Sharks are older than trees as a species.
Sharks have existed for roughly 450 million years; trees only appeared about 360 million years ago.
Humans have a stronger sense of smell than dogs.
Dogs have up to 300 million olfactory receptors vs. humans' 6 million, giving them a far superior sense of smell.
The moon is slowly moving away from Earth.
The moon drifts about 3.8 cm farther from Earth each year due to tidal interactions.
Sunflowers track the sun throughout the day.
Young sunflowers follow the sun (heliotropism); mature ones typically face east permanently.
Lightning strikes Earth about 100 times per second on average.
Roughly 8 million lightning strikes hit Earth every day — that's about 100 per second.
The hardest natural material after diamond is graphene.
After diamond, the next hardest natural mineral is generally moissanite (silicon carbide).
The tongue is the strongest muscle in the human body.
The masseter (jaw muscle) is often cited as the strongest by force; the tongue is not technically a single muscle.
The human eye can distinguish over 10 million different colors.
The human visual system can theoretically distinguish between 10 million or more distinct colors.
Neutron stars are so dense that a teaspoon of their material weighs about a billion tons.
Neutron star matter is extraordinarily compressed — a teaspoon would weigh about 10 million tons.
Cats always land on their feet due to a reflex called 'aerial righting'.
Cats have a 'righting reflex' that allows them to rotate mid-fall to land feet first.
Glass is technically a very slow-moving liquid.
This is a popular myth; old glass being thicker at the bottom is due to manufacturing, not flow.
Honey bees must visit approximately 2 million flowers to make one pound of honey.
Bees travel enormous cumulative distances and visit millions of flowers to produce honey.
There are more atoms in a glass of water than glasses of water in all Earth's oceans.
A glass of water contains roughly 10²⁵ molecules — far more than the number of glassfuls in all the oceans.
A mitochondrion can make copies of itself independently of the cell.
Mitochondria have their own DNA and divide independently, supporting the endosymbiotic theory of their origin.
The Earth's inner core rotates slightly faster than the rest of the planet.
Scientific studies suggest the inner core rotates at a slightly different rate than the outer layers.
Elephants are the only animals that cannot jump.
Many animals cannot jump, including hippos, rhinos, and sloths — not just elephants.
Human fingernails grow faster on the dominant hand.
Research shows nails grow slightly faster on the hand you use more, likely due to increased blood flow.

fact_or_fake: The Great Wall of China took over 1,000 years to build.
Construction spanned from the 7th century BC to the 17th century AD — over 1,000 years of various dynasties building and extending it.
Julius Caesar was born by caesarean section.
The 'Caesarean' name likely comes from a Latin root — Caesar's mother survived his birth, which would not have happened if C-sections were performed then.
The ancient Egyptians used toothpaste.
They used a paste made from crushed rock salt, mint, dried iris flower, and pepper.
Vikings wore horned helmets.
No archaeological evidence supports horned Viking helmets — that's a 19th-century myth popularized by artists.
The Trojan War was entirely fictional with no historical basis.
Archaeological evidence at Hisarlik in Turkey suggests a real conflict around 1200 BC that likely inspired the legend.
Cleopatra was Egyptian by blood.
Cleopatra was of Macedonian Greek descent, from the Ptolemaic dynasty.
Ancient Greeks had a word for being bored.
Ancient Greek had no single word equivalent to modern boredom — the concept as we know it emerged much later.
The Black Death was caused by a bacterium, not a virus.
The Black Death was caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium spread by fleas on rats.
Napoleon was unusually short for his time.
He stood around 5'7'' — average for a French man of his era. The myth came partly from a British propaganda nickname.
The Eiffel Tower was built as a permanent Parisian landmark.
It was originally intended to be a temporary structure for the 1889 World's Fair and was nearly demolished.
Ancient Romans used urine as a mouthwash.
The ammonia in urine was valued as a cleaning agent, and Roman toothpaste and mouthwash recipes included it.
King Tutankhamun died in battle.
Evidence suggests he died from complications of malaria combined with a broken leg, likely not in battle.
The first printed book was the Gutenberg Bible.
Johannes Gutenberg's Bible, printed around 1455, is considered the first major book printed using movable type in Europe.
Ancient Mayans invented the concept of zero.
The Maya independently developed a positional number system that included zero, around the 4th century AD.
The Statue of Liberty was originally intended for Egypt.
The sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi originally pitched a similar design to Egypt for the Suez Canal before proposing it to the USA.
The hundred years war lasted exactly 100 years.
The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453.
Ancient Greeks invented the first alarm clock.
Ctesibius of Alexandria invented a water clock that could ring an alarm, around 250 BC.
Marie Curie is the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
She won the Nobel Prize in Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911).
The first Olympics only allowed married women to compete.
Married women were actually forbidden from attending or competing; only unmarried women could attend certain events.
The Wright Brothers' first flight lasted less than a minute.
Orville Wright's first controlled flight at Kitty Hawk in 1903 lasted just 12 seconds.
Ancient Egyptians shaved their eyebrows when their cat died.
As a sign of mourning for the sacred animal, family members would shave their eyebrows.
The word 'salary' comes from 'sal', the Latin word for salt.
Roman soldiers were sometimes paid in salt, giving us the word 'salary'.
The first woman to run for U.S. President did so before women could vote.
Victoria Woodhull ran for president in 1872, nearly 50 years before women's suffrage was granted.
Shakespeare invented over 1,700 words still used in English today.
Words like 'bedroom', 'lonely', 'generous', and 'gloomy' are among those attributed to Shakespeare.
The Colosseum in Rome was used as a quarry in the Middle Ages.
Romans recycled its travertine stone for other buildings, taking roughly 100,000 tonnes of material.
Christopher Columbus was trying to prove the Earth was round.
Educated people already knew the Earth was round — Columbus was trying to find a western sea route to Asia.
Ancient Spartans used iron bars as currency to discourage hoarding wealth.
Spartans deliberately used heavy, impractical iron bars to make wealth accumulation difficult.
The Black Death killed fewer than 10% of Europe's population.
The Black Death killed an estimated 30–60% of Europe's population in the 14th century.
The term 'assassin' comes from an Arabic word related to hashish.
The word derives from 'hashishin', a name given to the Nizari Ismailis, though the drug link is historically disputed.
Medieval peasants had no concept of vacation or leisure time.
Medieval peasants had numerous religious feast days and market days that served as communal rest and celebration.

fact_or_fake: The first text message ever sent said 'Merry Christmas'.
Neil Papworth sent 'Merry Christmas' to Vodafone director Richard Jarvis on 3 December 1992.
Tamagotchis were invented in Japan in the 1990s.
Bandai released the Tamagotchi in Japan in 1996, creating a global virtual pet craze.
The Lion King was the first Disney film based on an original story.
Many Disney films before it were original stories; The Lion King was also heavily inspired by Shakespeare's Hamlet and a Japanese anime.
The Spice Girls sold more albums in the 1990s than any other female group in history.
Wannabe debuted at number one in 37 countries and the group became the best-selling female group of all time.
The first Harry Potter book was rejected by 12 publishers before being accepted.
J.K. Rowling faced multiple rejections before Bloomsbury published Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone in 1997.
The PlayStation 1 was originally designed as a CD-ROM add-on for the Super Nintendo.
Sony developed it in partnership with Nintendo before the deal fell through, leading to the standalone PlayStation.
Friends was the highest-rated TV show of the entire 1990s decade.
ER was actually the top-rated show for most of the 90s, though Friends was hugely popular.
The internet was available to the public before the 1990s.
The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 and became publicly available in 1991, though widespread home use exploded in the mid-90s.
Kurt Cobain named Nirvana after a Buddhist concept meaning transcendence.
Cobain confirmed he chose the name for its spiritual connotation of freedom from suffering.
Space Jam featured Michael Jordan's actual basketball skills motion-captured for the animated scenes.
Space Jam used traditional animation; motion capture technology wasn't used for Jordan in that film.
The first Google search engine was launched from a garage in 1998.
Larry Page and Sergey Brin launched Google in 1998, initially working out of a garage in Menlo Park.
Furby was originally designed for the Japanese market.
Furby was an American creation by Tiger Electronics, first released in 1998 and then sold worldwide.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in the 1990s.
Hubble was launched on April 24, 1990, aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery.
Windows 95 sold more than a million copies in its first week.
It sold around 7 million copies in the first five weeks — a record-breaking launch for software at the time.
The Mighty Morphin Power Rangers were originally a Japanese show.
They were adapted from the Japanese 'Super Sentai' series, with new footage of American actors spliced in.
Titanic (1997) was the first film to earn $1 billion at the global box office.
It became the highest-grossing film of all time at that point, earning over $1.8 billion globally.
The yo-yo was originally a weapon before it became a toy.
Despite the popular story, there is no credible historical evidence that yo-yos were used as weapons.
Slap bracelets were banned in some US schools in the early 1990s.
Multiple schools banned them after reports of children getting cuts from the exposed metal inside worn bracelets.
The first ever DVD movie released was Twister.
Twister was the first DVD movie released in the United States in March 1997.
The 90s hit song 'Macarena' was originally a slow ballad.
Los del Río originally recorded it as a slower, more traditional flamenco-pop song before it was remixed into the dance hit.
Beanie Babies were so popular in the 90s that people invested millions in them expecting them to gain value.
The beanie baby craze led people to buy, collect, and store them in protective cases, expecting huge returns — most were ultimately worth very little.
The Goosebumps book series was created by R.L. Stine in the 1990s.
R.L. Stine launched the Goosebumps series in 1992, and it became one of the best-selling book series of all time.
Bill Nye the Science Guy first aired on TV in 1993.
Bill Nye the Science Guy premiered on September 10, 1993 on KCTS in Seattle.
The Backstreet Boys were put together through an open audition in New York.
They were formed in Orlando, Florida in 1993 through connections made by businessman Lou Pearlman.
Pokémon was originally called 'Capsule Monsters'.
Creator Satoshi Tajiri originally proposed the concept under the working title 'Capsule Monsters' before it became Pocket Monsters/Pokémon.
The Matrix was the first film to use bullet-time photography.
The Wachowskis pioneered the technique for The Matrix (1999) using dozens of still cameras firing in sequence.
The original Game Boy had a color screen.
The original Game Boy, released in 1989, had a distinctive yellow-green monochrome screen. The Game Boy Color didn't arrive until 1998.
AOL Instant Messenger launched in the 1990s.
AIM launched in 1997 and became one of the dominant ways people communicated online through the late 90s and 2000s.
Shrek was originally planned as a 2D animated film.
DreamWorks initially developed Shrek as a 2D film before switching to 3D CGI animation.
Fresh Prince of Bel-Air's theme song was improvised by Will Smith in under an hour.
Smith has claimed he wrote and recorded the theme song in about an hour during a studio session.

fact_or_fake: Russia is so large it spans 11 time zones.
Russia is the largest country by area and covers 11 different time zones.
Australia is the only country that is also a continent.
Australia is unique in being both a country and its own continent.
The Amazon River discharges more freshwater than the next seven largest rivers combined.
The Amazon accounts for approximately 20% of all freshwater discharged into the oceans globally.
The Dead Sea is the lowest point on Earth's land surface.
At roughly 430 metres below sea level, the Dead Sea is Earth's lowest land surface point.
Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined.
Canada contains about 60% of the world's lakes, with estimates exceeding 2 million.
The Pacific Ocean is larger than all of Earth's landmass combined.
The Pacific Ocean covers about 165 million km², more than all the continents put together.
China shares a border with more countries than any other nation.
Russia shares land borders with 14 countries — the same count as China, tied for most.
The Nile River flows northward.
The Nile flows south to north, emptying into the Mediterranean Sea in northern Egypt.
New Zealand was the last large habitable land on Earth to be settled by humans.
The Māori arrived around 1280 AD, making New Zealand one of the last major landmasses to be settled.
Iceland is covered mostly in ice and Greenland is mostly green.
Iceland has relatively mild coasts due to the Gulf Stream, while much of Greenland is ice sheet.
The Great Barrier Reef is visible from space.
The reef is around 2,300 km long, making it visible from low orbit.
Vatican City has no permanent residents.
Vatican City has several hundred permanent residents, including clergy, the Swiss Guard, and service workers.
Mount Everest grows taller every year due to tectonic activity.
The Indian and Eurasian plates continue to push together, adding approximately 4mm to Everest's height annually.
The Sahara Desert is getting larger due to desertification.
The Sahara has expanded southward by roughly 10% since 1920 due to climate change and land use.
Brazil is the only Portuguese-speaking country in South America.
All other South American countries speak Spanish as their primary language, except for Brazil.
The capital of Australia is Sydney.
The capital of Australia is Canberra, which was purpose-built as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.
The world's smallest country is Monaco.
Vatican City, at 0.44 km², is smaller than Monaco.
The Mississippi River flows south into the Gulf of Mexico.
The Mississippi begins in Minnesota and flows southward for approximately 3,730 km to the Gulf of Mexico.
More than half of the world's countries are in the Southern Hemisphere.
The majority of countries are in the Northern Hemisphere; only around 30-35 countries lie mostly south of the equator.
Finland has more saunas than cars.
Finland has approximately 3.3 million saunas for a population of 5.5 million — more than the number of registered cars.
The Atacama Desert in South America receives virtually no rain.
Some parts of the Atacama haven't seen measurable rainfall in centuries, making it the driest non-polar desert.
The Caspian Sea is technically the world's largest lake.
The Caspian Sea, although called a sea, is landlocked and classified by some geographers as a lake.
Nepal and China share the summit of Mount Everest.
The border runs roughly through the summit, meaning both countries can technically claim Everest's peak.
The Danube River flows through more countries than any other river.
The Danube passes through or borders 10 countries in Europe — more than any other river.
Antarctica has no permanent human population but does have permanent research stations.
No indigenous population lives in Antarctica, but around 1,000–5,000 researchers live there depending on the season.
The population of Tokyo is greater than the entire population of Canada.
Greater Tokyo has over 37 million people; Canada's population is approximately 38–40 million — very close.
Every country in the world has at least one mountain.
Countries like Bangladesh, Maldives, and parts of the Netherlands are almost entirely flat with no mountains.
Lake Baikal contains more freshwater than all of North America's Great Lakes combined.
Lake Baikal holds approximately 23% of the world's surface freshwater — more than the five Great Lakes together.
The equator passes through 13 countries.
The equator crosses through Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, São Tomé & Príncipe, Gabon, Congo, DRC, Uganda, Kenya, Somalia, Maldives, Indonesia, and Kiribati.
The world's longest coastline belongs to Canada.
Canada's coastline measures approximately 202,080 km — the longest of any country.

fact_or_fake: Santa Claus's red suit was created by Coca-Cola's advertising team.
The red suit predates Coca-Cola's 1930s ads — it was popularized by earlier illustrators like Thomas Nast in the 19th century.
Christmas was once banned in England.
Under Oliver Cromwell in the 1640s and 1650s, Christmas celebrations were illegal in England.
The first Christmas card was sent in 1843.
Sir Henry Cole commissioned the first commercial Christmas card in 1843 in England.
Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer was originally created by a department store.
Rudolph was created in 1939 by Robert L. May for Montgomery Ward stores as a holiday promotional giveaway.
Christmas trees originated in Germany.
The tradition of decorating Christmas trees originated in Germany in the 16th century and spread globally.
Jingle Bells was originally written as a Thanksgiving song.
James Lord Pierpont wrote it in 1857 for a Thanksgiving celebration — the lyrics reference horse racing, not Christmas.
The world's tallest Christmas tree ever displayed was over 200 feet tall.
A Douglas fir displayed in a Washington state shopping center in 1950 measured 221 feet.
Boxing Day gets its name from boxing matches held on the 26th of December.
Boxing Day likely comes from the tradition of giving gift boxes to servants or tradespeople, not from the sport.
In Japan, it's traditional to eat KFC for Christmas.
A 1974 marketing campaign turned KFC into a beloved Japanese Christmas tradition — orders are placed months in advance.
Candy canes were invented to keep children quiet in church during long Christmas services.
One account traces the origin to a choirmaster at Cologne Cathedral in Germany who gave sugar sticks to children.
The famous Christmas song 'White Christmas' was written by a Jewish songwriter.
Irving Berlin, who was Jewish, wrote 'White Christmas' — still the best-selling single of all time.
The tradition of leaving out milk and cookies for Santa comes from Norse mythology.
The most likely origin is Dutch and Scandinavian traditions of leaving out food for Odin's horse, Sleipnir.
Eggnog originated in North America in the 1700s.
Eggnog developed in early America from British milk-and-ale drinks like posset, with rum replacing ale.
In Australia, Christmas falls during summer.
Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere, so December 25 is in the middle of their summer.
The song 'Happy Birthday to You' earns more royalties than any Christmas song annually.
Until it entered the public domain in 2016, 'Happy Birthday' consistently earned more royalties than seasonal songs.
Santa Claus is based on a real historical person.
Santa Claus is based on Saint Nicholas of Myra, a 4th-century Christian bishop known for generosity.
Hanukkah always falls on the same date in December.
Hanukkah follows the Hebrew calendar and can fall anywhere from late November to late December.
The Christmas stocking tradition comes from a story about Saint Nicholas throwing gold coins.
Legend says Saint Nicholas tossed bags of gold through a window, landing in stockings hung to dry.
Mistletoe was considered sacred by the ancient Celts and Norse.
Both cultures considered mistletoe a powerful symbol of peace, love, and protection.
Christmas became a federal holiday in the USA in 1870.
President Ulysses S. Grant signed Christmas into law as a US federal holiday on June 28, 1870.
The traditional 12 Days of Christmas start on Christmas Day.
Traditionally the 12 Days of Christmas begin on December 25 and end on January 5 (Twelfth Night).
Poinsettias are poisonous to humans.
They can cause mild stomach upset, but poinsettias are not dangerously toxic to humans, though they can be irritating.
The world's most expensive Christmas tree was decorated with diamonds and cost over $11 million.
A tree in Abu Dhabi in 2010 was decorated with $11 million worth of jewels and ornaments.
Elves are a traditional part of Scandinavian Christmas folklore.
Tomte or Nisse — small elf-like figures — have been part of Scandinavian Christmas tradition for centuries.
Christmas was not widely celebrated in America until the mid-1800s.
Puritan influence suppressed Christmas celebration in early America; it only gained wider popularity after the 1820s–1840s.
Tinsel was originally made of real silver.
Tinsel was first made from thin strips of hammered real silver in Germany in the 17th century.
The Christmas cracker was invented by a British confectioner in the 1840s.
Tom Smith invented the Christmas cracker in 1847, inspired by French bonbons wrapped in paper.
Reindeer are real animals and both males and females can grow antlers.
Rangifer tarandus is a real animal; uniquely among deer, females also grow antlers.
In Iceland, 13 different Santas (called Yule Lads) visit children in December.
Icelandic Christmas folklore includes 13 Yule Lads, each with a different mischievous trait.
The date December 25 was chosen for Christmas because it was the known birth date of Jesus.
No historical record confirms Jesus's birth date; December 25 was likely chosen to coincide with existing winter solstice celebrations.
